articleTitle: Presidential address
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: My mind was not entirely free from misgivings when I was faced with the question on occupying the presidential chair of this Institute during the coming year, for while I appreciate the honour done to me by the Council and members of the Institute in electing me to this position — an honour for which I wish to express my gratitude and appreciation, and an honour which I appreciate the more in that it is conferred on me by my fellow-members of the electrical engineering fraternity, I am, nevertheless, fully cognisant of the responsibility which this position carries with it and which cannot be taken lightly. This, together with the fact that the programme of development before the Electricity Supply Commission at the present time places a tremendous responsibility upon my shoulders and a severe tax on time and energy, brought home to me the realisation that I shall have to make special efforts to conduct the affairs of this Institute in a manner commensurate with the standard set by my predecessors.

articleTitle: Bloemfontein new power station
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Bloemfontein Electricity Undertaking was first opened in 1900, the generating plant at that time having a capacity of 180 K.W. After various extensions, the plant capacity in 1921 reached 2,600 K.W., and the output in 1923 amounted to 4·23 millions K.W.H. sold. In that year my firm, Messrs. G. M. Clark & Partner, were asked to prepare a report in conjunction with Mr. Macaulay, the City Electrical Engineer, on the undertaking. Our joint recommendation to build a new power station was adopted, and the new power station was put into commission in the early part of this year. Mr. Hammond, the consulting engineer in 1900, advised that the Bloemfontein Council should instal an A.C. 50-cycle, three-phase scheme, instead of the more general direct-current system then in vogue. This recommendation, having been adopted, proved to be the best system for general utility, and obviated the necessity of installing expensive converting plant at a later date.

abstract: A few historical notes on the development of the Berlin Electricity Undertaking may be of interest. The electricity works in Berlin were formed as a public share company in 1884 by the German Edison Company, which developed soon afterwards into the Allgemeine Elektricitaets-Gesell-schaft (A.E.G.). It was the first public supply company in Germany and was the sole undertaking authorised in Berlin for the supply of electrical energy. The municipality had the option of purchasing the undertaking after a certain number of years, but it was not until 1915 that this option was exercised.

It is interesting to know that one of our keenest students of the problem of drilling holes in rock, Mr. Henry S. Potter, during his recent overseas visit got into touch with Dr. Japolsky and gave him the essential outline of a jack-hammer type of drill, suitable for the application of variable-frequency currents, which would be useable on these fields without in any way conflicting with present practice. articleTitle: Wired wireless—(Continuation)
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: In adding to my paper on the application of the h.f. carrier system of telephony over the 132 k.v. transmission line between Witbank and Brakpan and its extension to the ordinary. telephone system, I may at the outset state that, after a further 12 months' experience, we have overcome practically all the ordinary apparatus trouble, and for the last six or eight months breakdown has been very rare indeed and the maintenance extremely small in comparison to the very large use made of the system. As an interesting fact bearing on this, recently, during experimental trials of the imported sets now being installed, records were taken of the use during normal periods, and over a period of 106 hours 355 conversations were registered. When it is realised that, during periods when switching operations are taking place, some of these calls demand that the gear is in constant operation for anything from 15 to 45 minutes (48 minutes has been recorded), one feels quite satisfied that this system of communication, standing up as it does, is quite adequate to meet any requirements. I propose later to deal with the various items in the apparatus and our experience with them, and the methods to be adopted in order to obtain gear which is in every way as reliable as any single long trunk line, with the added advantage, which will readily be appreciated, that all troubles are confined to the two transmitting sets at each end, which are readily accessible.
